source_read: PDF, printed pp. 539-542 in full (pp. 542 is the start of an unrelated article); Table I (p. 540) and Table II (p. 541) checked on pages rendered at 150 and 300 dpi because the machine-read text of this scanned article garbles the table rows

claims.overstatement: No. The claim keeps the figures tied to their conditions (0.5 mg/kg intramuscular or oral solution against an intravenous dose in the same person), names the sample size of four for both headline figures, and does not generalise beyond the volunteers studied. No dose is given other than as a study condition.
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this source was found and recomputed. Means and standard errors recomputed from the per-subject values printed in Table I: intramuscular 0.965, 0.923, 0.972, 0.859 give mean 0.9298 (SE 0.0260), printed 0.930 (0.026); oral 0.145, 0.163, 0.112, 0.245 give mean 0.1663 (SE 0.0283), printed 0.166 (0.028); the six Eq. 2 values 0.160, 0.190, 0.155, 0.115, 0.309, 0.239 give mean 0.1947 (SE 0.0284), printed 0.195 (0.028). All three reproduce. Two small corrections of emphasis: (a) the 'failure to absorb' wording is not confined to the abstract, the Results (p. 540) also say absorption was incomplete, so the contradiction is between the abstract and Results on one side and the Discussion on the other; (b) the claim's 'four people' is right because Table I prints no bioavailability for subjects 3 and 5. No confidence interval appears anywhere in the paper, as the claim says; dispersion is given as standard error throughout.

anchors.locator: Table I (Farea columns for the intramuscular injection and the oral solution, and the F (Eq. 2) column)
anchors.extracted: Bioavailability of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg against the same person's intravenous curve. Intramuscular Farea in four of six people: 0.965, 0.923, 0.972, 0.859; mean 0.930, SE 0.026. Oral solution Farea in the same four: 0.145, 0.163, 0.112, 0.245; mean 0.166, SE 0.028. A second oral calculation (Eq. 2, assuming complete absorption from the gut) is printed for all six: 0.160, 0.190, 0.155, 0.115, 0.309, 0.239; mean 0.195, SE 0.028. Subjects 3 and 5 have no Farea for either route. Editors' recomputation of all three means and standard errors from the printed per-subject values reproduces the printed values.

anchors.locator: Table II, ketamine block (Cmax and tmax rows)
anchors.extracted: Mean (SE), n = 6 per the table footnote: peak plasma ketamine 243 (49) ng/mL at 22 (4) min after the 0.5 mg/kg intramuscular injection, and 44 (10) ng/mL at 30 (5) min after the 0.5 mg/kg oral solution; no Cmax or tmax is printed for the intravenous condition. Dose-corrected area under the curve 27.5 (1.2) intravenous, 23.6 (2.2) intramuscular, 4.8 (0.8) oral min ng/mL.

anchors.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs of the right-hand column
anchors.extracted: After the intramuscular injection the estimated lag time between injection and the appearance of ketamine in plasma was under 4 minutes and apparent peak concentrations of between 100 and 425 ng/mL occurred at 5 to 30 minutes. After the oral solution absorption was described as incomplete with only 16.6% of the dose reaching the systemic circulation, lag time 4 to 13 minutes (mean 8.0), and a mean apparent peak of 44 ng/mL (range 15 to 80 ng/mL) against 243 ng/mL after the intramuscular injection.

anchors.locator: Abstract, 1st paragraph, read against p. 541 Discussion, 1st paragraph of the right-hand column
anchors.extracted: The abstract states that only 17% of an oral dose was absorbed because of extensive first-pass metabolism, and the Results (p. 540) likewise call absorption incomplete. The Discussion argues the opposite mechanism: because the dose-corrected areas under the norketamine curve were similar after all three routes, the low plasma ketamine concentrations are attributed solely to first-pass metabolism, and the Eq. 2 calculation (which assumes absorption from the gut lumen was complete) agreed with the area-based figure.

anchors.locator: Experimental > Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, read against p. 540 Experimental > Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 3rd paragraph, and the Table II footnote on p. 541
anchors.extracted: Two studies: five healthy fasting volunteers (mean age 33.8, SE 1.4 years; weight 74.8, SE 2.1 kg) received intravenous ketamine 0.25 or 0.125 mg/kg and saline on separate occasions; six healthy fasting volunteers (age 31.8, SE 2.0 years; weight 70.7, SE 4.4 kg) received 0.5 mg/kg intramuscularly or as an oral solution in orange juice, with saline, in crossover with randomised order and with the participant and the person scoring pain unaware of the solution. Bioavailability is defined as the ratio of the area after the intramuscular or oral dose to that after intravenous injection in the same subject, but no table says which people contributed the intravenous reference, and the Table II footnote states N = 6 for all three routes including the intravenous column, which the five-person first study does not support.

claims.overstatement: Two places. First, the claim says the intramuscular half-life (155 min) and the oral half-life (174 min) 'did not differ significantly' from the intravenous one; the paper tests and reports this only for the intramuscular condition (p. 540), and prints no comparison for the oral half-life. Second, the closing sentence that how long ketamine lasts after being swallowed 'is not reported in either study' is contradicted by this paper, which prints a terminal half-life of 174 min (SE 50) after the oral solution in Table II (p. 541). The rest of the wording is faithful: norketamine areas are reported as similar and not significantly different, and the first-pass reading is given as the authors' interpretation.
claims.note: All numbers taken from this source were found and match: 186 min with SE 10 in the Results text (p. 540) and SE 8 in Table II (p. 541), a real internal inconsistency; clearance 19.1 (1.1) intravenous and 23.2 (2.7) intramuscular mL/min/kg; intramuscular half-life 155 (12); oral half-life 174 (50); norketamine peaks 40 (6), 92 (10), 200 (44) ng/mL at 63 (23), 78 (14) and 60 (13) min, with dose-corrected areas 35.4 (3.8), 31.3 (3.8) and 36.7 (3.9) min ng/mL. The claim's two-phase description matches the fitted two-compartment model and the printed equations. Note that the whole terminal-half-life set rests on n = 6 per the Table II footnote while the intravenous condition is described as a five-person study (p. 539).

anchors.extracted: After intravenous injection plasma ketamine fell rapidly and was fitted by a two-compartment open model with a mean terminal half-life of 186 (SE 10) min; the printed biexponential equations are y = 82 exp(-0.044t) + 22 exp(-0.0039t) after 0.125 mg/kg and y = 108 exp(-0.039t) + 40 exp(-0.0038t) after 0.25 mg/kg, with no significant differences between the two doses in alpha, beta, apparent distribution volumes or clearance.

anchors.locator: Table II (half-life, AUC and TBC rows for ketamine; Cmax, tmax and AUC rows for norketamine)
anchors.extracted: Mean (SE), n = 6 per footnote. Ketamine terminal half-life 186 (8) min intravenous, 155 (12) intramuscular, 174 (50) oral; clearance not corrected for bioavailability 19.1 (1.1) and 23.2 (2.7) mL/min/kg, none printed for the oral route. Norketamine peak 40 (6), 92 (10) and 200 (44) ng/mL at 63 (23), 78 (14) and 60 (13) min; dose-corrected areas 35.4 (3.8), 31.3 (3.8) and 36.7 (3.9) min ng/mL. The table's standard error for the intravenous half-life (8) differs from the 10 printed in the Results on p. 540.

anchors.locator: Results > Pharmacokinetics, 3rd paragraph of the right-hand column
anchors.extracted: The mean (SE) terminal half-life after the intramuscular injection, 155 (12) min, is stated not to differ significantly from the intravenous value of 186 (10) min, with no difference in clearance (23.2 and 19.1 mL/min/kg). No corresponding comparison is printed for the oral half-life anywhere in the paper; the Student t test is named as the test used (p. 540) but no test statistic or p value is given for any pharmacokinetic comparison.

anchors.locator: Table II, ketamine half-life row, oral column
anchors.extracted: A terminal half-life of 174 min (SE 50) is printed for the 0.5 mg/kg oral solution, so this study does report how long ketamine persists after a swallowed dose, contrary to the claim's closing sentence.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph of the right-hand column
anchors.extracted: The authors read the similar dose-corrected norketamine areas as showing that the swallowed dose was absorbed and then metabolised in the liver before reaching the circulation, invoking the principle that the metabolite's area is independent of route when the liver is the sole site of metabolism; the metabolite peak after the oral dose (200 ng/mL) exceeded that after the intramuscular one (92 ng/mL) while the areas were similar.

Table I values and the mean 0.930 (SE 0.026) verified; my own recomputation from 0.965, 0.923, 0.972 and 0.859 gives 0.9298 and SE 0.0260, so the card's editors' calculation holds and n = 4 is right.

Verified at Table I (p. 540), Results 3rd paragraph (p. 540) and Discussion 3rd paragraph (p. 541). My recomputation reproduces both means and standard errors (0.1663, SE 0.0283 on four values; 0.1947, SE 0.0284 on six), confirming n = 4 and n = 6.
All Table II values verified on the page rendered at 300 dpi, the text layer of this scanned page being unreliable. The notes on the area unit and on the N = 6 footnote are both correct.

Figure 1 is on p. 539 and the concentrations 186 (SE 23) and 101 (SE 8) ng/mL are in Results > Pain Measurements, 3rd paragraph (p. 541). Counting the rendered figure myself I make it about 10 points in panel (a) and about 17 in panel (b), which matches the card's approximate counts.
r = 0.712 and p < 0.001 are printed inside Figure 2 on p. 540 and were legible on the page rendered at 150 dpi; I confirm the text layer loses both decimal points.
Verified: the intravenous durations carry citation 14 and the saline comparison citation 11, both companion papers of 1981.

Verified at Results 2nd paragraph (p. 540) and Discussion 5th paragraph (p. 541). Worth adding: the paper states this non-difference for the intramuscular route only, and prints no test for the oral half-life.

reporting_issues.note: The Results give 186 with SE 10 twice on p. 540, as the card says.
Found independently in the blind reading; the later review does record the intravenous row as n = 5 (Peltoniemi et al. 2016, Table 1).
Found independently in the blind reading.

My own calculation agrees: 0.5 mg/kg divided by 19.1 mL/min/kg is 26.2 micrograms*min/mL against a printed 27.5, so the tabulated areas are consistent with clearance but the printed unit is about a thousandfold too small.

Eq. 1 is introduced on p. 540 as the fraction lost to first-pass metabolism but written as 1 - TBC/Q1, which is the fraction escaping it, and Table I compares that column with the area-based bioavailability.

Correct in substance, but the abstract is not the only place: the Results on p. 540 also say absorption was incomplete, with only 16.6% reaching the systemic circulation. The contradiction is therefore between the abstract and the Results on one side and the Discussion on the other, which matters because a claim that quotes only the abstract against the Discussion understates how far the wording spread through the paper.

Counts agree within the card's own 'roughly' and 'about': I make it about 10 points in panel (a), about 17 in panel (b) and roughly two dozen in Figure 2, from six people, with no degrees of freedom printed.

Table I omits the Loo-Riegelman constant for subjects 3 (0.412, the highest nonlinear-regression value) and 5 (0.069); 0.069 is the third lowest of the six, so 'among the lowest' is the right phrasing.

The Introduction (p. 539) attributes the 2.5 mg/kg five-patient study with a 2.52 h half-life to reference 3, while the Discussion (p. 541) cites reference 14 for anaesthetic amounts and a 151 min half-life, the same figure.
No volume of distribution is printed anywhere, and I found no ethics or consent statement in the four printed pages.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 is the right instrument for a randomised-order crossover laboratory study under METHODS section 5.3, the domain judgments are supported by the text, and the overall judgment of high is not less severe than the worst domain. I would add one sentence to the measurement domain: the sampling schedule ran to 7 hours against a terminal half-life of about 3 hours, which the authors themselves show matters, since truncating their own intravenous data to 2 to 2.5 hours gives an apparent half-life of 105 minutes instead of 186 (p. 541).

interpretation_gap.note: The three gaps named are all in the paper: the abstract's absorption wording against the Discussion's first-pass argument, the headline 93% and 17% resting on four people with the sample size visible only in Table I, and the closing sentence about designing dosage regimens from an experimental ischaemic pain model in six healthy volunteers. 'Substantial' is the right rating.

missed: The paper's own demonstration that sampling length determines the half-life: analysing only the first 2 to 2.5 hours of its intravenous data gives an apparent half-life of 105 minutes against the 186 it reports (p. 541, Discussion 1st paragraph). This is the paper's explanation for a much shorter published figure and it is the right caution for comparing this half-life with studies that sample for 8 hours or less.

No key finding or reporting issue records that the paper tests the intramuscular half-life against the intravenous one but prints no comparison at all for the oral half-life of 174 minutes (SE 50), whose standard error is about a third of the mean. A claim that says all three half-lives did not differ significantly is reading the intramuscular sentence as covering the oral condition.
Table II prints no time to peak and no peak concentration for the intravenous condition, so the only within-paper comparison of peak heights is intramuscular against oral.
